astrolabie.def: The most important part of the 'astrolabe planisphere' consisted of a somewhat heavy circular plate of metal from four to seven inches in diameter

suffisaunt.def: In the best instruments, the Almicanteras, or circles of altitude, were drawn at distances of one degree only; in less-carefully made instruments, they were drawn at distances of two degrees. The one given to his son by Chaucer was one of the latter

latitude-t.gloss: the distance of any place on the globe, N. or S. of the equator

latitude-a.gloss: the angular distance of any body from the ecliptic
latitude-a.def: the angular distance of any body from the ecliptic, measured along a great circle at right angles to the ecliptic

conclusions.def: mathematical propositions, either problems or theorems

certein.def: a certein, i.e. a certain number; but the word nombre need not be repeated

bihestes.def: promises, i. e. what they profess to prove

ocrFixes: Hem, 2)ron. p)lthem → Hem, pron. pl. them

ref.head: Writen
ocrFixes: WrUen, pt. pi. wrote → Writen, pt. pl. wrote

excused.def: to have for excused, i. e. to excuse

con.def: To con one thanks, Fr. savoir gre, to feel thankful and make the feeling known to the object of it.

ref.head: Vsurpe
ocrFixes: Vsiirpe, 1 J), s. p)r. → Vsurpe, 1 p. s. pr.

declinacions.gloss: the angular distance of a celestial object N. or S. of the equator
declinacions.def: the angular distance of a celestial object N. or S. of the equator, measured along an arc at right angles to it

altitude.gloss: the elevation of a celestial object above the horizon
altitude.def: the elevation of a celestial object above the horizon, measured along a vertical arc

meridian.def: meridional, at the moment of southing, exact southern

kalendres.def: The old calendars answered nearly to our modern almanacks.

somer.def: The Kalendar of John Somer is extant in MS. Cotton, Vesp. E. vii. It is calculated for 140 years from 1367

lenne.def: Nicolaus de Lynna, i.e. of Lynn, in Norfolk, was a noted astrologer in the reign of Edward III., and was himself a writer of a treatise on the Astrolabe.

zodiac.def: An imaginary belt in the heavens, of the breadth of 12°, along the middle of which runs the ecliptic.

ecliptik.def: A great circle of the sphere, drawn along the middle of the zodiac, making an angle with the equator of about 23°. 28'; the apparent path of the sun, nearly.

equacions.def: The " equations of houses " means the method of dividing the sphere equally into "houses" for astrological purposes

houses.def: The whole celestial sphere was divided into twelve equal portions, called houses, by six great circles passing through the north and south points of the horizon

dignetes.def: the advantages which a planet has on account of being in a particular place in the zodiac, or in such a station with other planets

ref.head: Vouche
ocrFixes: Youclie, V. to vouch → Vouche, v. to vouch

rewle.gloss: the revolving long and narrow plate or rod used for measuring and taking altitudes

ref.head: Rewle
ocrFixes: long and 2l6 narrow → long and narrow

rewle.def: At the back of the astrolabe revolved the 'rule,' made of metal, and fitted with sights

maner.def: used without of following, as maner turet, kind of " turet,"

turet.gloss: the eye in which the ring of the Astrolabe turned
turet.def: It seems to mean both a ring which turns round, and an eye in which a ring can turn.

moder.def: the thickest plate forming the body or principal part of the Astrolabe

ref.head: Resseyuyth
ocrFixes: Resseyuy th, jj>r. s. → Resseyuyth, pr. s.

wombe.gloss: the depression in the front of an astrolabe

clymatz.gloss: climates, i. e. zones of latitude
clymatz.def: sometimes an instrument was provided with several of them, differently marked, for use in places having different latitudes

riet.def: The 'rete' or 'net' is the circular plate with many openings which revolves within the 'mother.'
